# Events: Pointer Years and Superposed Epoch Analysis

:::{.callout-note title="Draft"}
First draft, 2026-10-28, replacing the stub. Every number in the text is computed when the book builds. Open questions are in the backlog.
:::

## Big Idea

Some years stand out across a whole stand. A late frost, a drought or a cold summer after a big eruption can leave a narrow ring in nearly every tree. Those years are useful. They are the signatures that crossdating leans on, and they are a record of the events themselves.

There are two ways to come at them. You can start from the trees and ask which years most of them agree were unusual. Those are pointer years, and `pointer` finds them. Or you can start from a list of events chosen in advance, eruptions or fires, and ask whether growth around those years differs from growth around any other years. That is superposed epoch analysis, and `sea` does it.

Both are easy to run and easy to over-read. This chapter plants cold years in a simulated stand and checks that each method finds them, and looks at what each one finds that I didn't plant. Then it turns both on field collections: `pointer` on Mesa Verde, where most years would count as pointer years at the default settings, and `sea` on a white spruce chronology from the Yukon with the coldest summers of the last 600 years as the events.

## Packages

```{r}
#| label: ev-setup
#| message: false
library(dplR)
library(ggplot2)
source("R/sim-collection.R")
data(co021)
data(cana157)
```

`ggplot2` draws the figures, and `R/sim-collection.R` is the book's simulator from [From Cores to a Record](02CoresToRecord.qmd). Everything else is `dplR` and base R.

```{r}
#| label: ev-words
#| include: false
# counts of zero to nine as words in the prose, larger ones as numerals
words <- function(n) {
  ifelse(n >= 0 & n <= 9,
         c("zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven",
           "eight", "nine")[n + 1], as.character(n))
}
pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
```

## Pointer Years

The terms come from a meeting in Lourmarin in 1989, written up by @Schweingruber1990. An event year is a conspicuous ring in one series. A pointer year is a year when many series in a group show an event year together [@Schweingruber1990, p. 19].

"Conspicuous" needs a rule. The one `pointer` uses is from @Becker1994, who called a year a pointer year when at least 70% of the trees had rings at least 10% narrower or wider than the year before (p. 480). `pointer` works the same way. For each series it divides each ring by the ring before, which it calls the relative growth variation. A ratio of 1.10 or more counts as a jump up and 0.90 or less as a drop, set by `rgv.thresh = 10`. A year is a negative pointer year when at least `nseries.thresh = 75` percent of the series dropped, and a positive one when that many jumped.

Two things follow from the ratio. A pointer year is about the change from the year before, so a narrow ring after another narrow ring isn't one. And a year with no ring before it in a series isn't counted for that series.

### A Stand with Planted Cold Years

To see whether `pointer` finds what it should, I'll plant some. The simulator takes a climate series if you give it one. Here it's white noise in standard units, with eight years set to three standard deviations below the mean.

```{r}
#| label: ev-sim
simYears <- 1600:2025
set.seed(10)
coldClimate <- rnorm(length(simYears))
names(coldClimate) <- simYears
coldYears <- c(1695, 1740, 1783, 1816, 1837, 1884, 1912, 1968)
coldClimate[as.character(coldYears)] <- -3
sim <- sim.collection(climate = coldClimate, event = NULL, release = NULL,
                      errors = NULL, seed = 1)
simRwl <- sim$rwl
```

`sim.collection` rescales the climate to its own variance and shares it among all the trees, and each tree's memory carries part of a bad year into the next. I turned off the release, the stand-wide disturbance and the dating error the simulator plants by default, so the only extremes the trees share are the climate's. The collection has `r ncol(simRwl)` cores from `r ncol(simRwl) / 2` trees.

```{r}
#| label: ev-sim-pointer
simPtr <- pointer(simRwl)
# the first rows of simRwl come before any core starts, so drop them
simPtr <- simPtr[simPtr$Nb.series > 0, ]
head(simPtr)
simNeg <- simPtr$Year[simPtr$Nature == -1]
simHits <- coldYears %in% simNeg
```

Each row is a year. `Nb.series` is how many series have a ratio that year, `Perc.pos` and `Perc.neg` are the percentages that jumped or dropped, and `Nature` is 1, −1 or 0 for a positive, negative or no pointer year. `RGV_mean` and `RGV_sd` are the mean and standard deviation of the ratios, as percent changes.

`pointer` found `r words(sum(simHits))` of the `r words(length(coldYears))` planted years. The one it missed, `r coldYears[!simHits]`, had `r simPtr$Perc.neg[simPtr$Year == coldYears[!simHits]]`% of its `r simPtr$Nb.series[simPtr$Year == coldYears[!simHits]]` series drop by 10% or more, short of 75%. It also found `r length(setdiff(simNeg, coldYears))` negative pointer years I didn't plant, and `r sum(simPtr$Nature == 1)` positive ones.

### How Many Series?

Some of those extra pointer years are near the start of the collection, where few series are in. With two series, "75% of the series" means both, and two series dropping together in a dry year is common. @Schweingruber1990 [p. 21] give a rule from Eckstein and Bauch for how many series have to agree before the agreement is unlikely by chance. If rises and falls are equally likely and the series are independent, the share that agree in a year rarely tops

$$
\left(0.5 + \frac{0.5}{n} + z\sqrt{\frac{0.25}{n}}\right) \times 100\%
$$

for $n$ series, with $z = 3.291$, the normal quantile for 99.9%. The limit can't be met below a certain depth, because it's over 100%.

```{r}
#| label: ev-depth-limit
pointerLimit <- function(n, z = 3.291) {
  100 * (0.5 + 0.5 / n + z * sqrt(0.25 / n))
}
minDepth <- min(which(pointerLimit(1:100) <= 100))
round(pointerLimit(c(minDepth, 20, 40)), 1)
```

Below `r minDepth` series, no share of agreeing series clears the limit. At `r minDepth` it takes `r round(pointerLimit(minDepth), 1)`%, at 20 series `r round(pointerLimit(20), 1)`%, and at 40 `r round(pointerLimit(40), 1)`%. `pointer`'s rule has a third category, rings that changed by less than 10%, so a random rise or fall of 10% is less likely than the 50:50 the formula assumes and the limit is on the cautious side. Even so, it's a reason to set aside pointer years where only a few series are in.

```{r}
#| label: ev-sim-deep
simPtr$deep <- simPtr$Nb.series >= minDepth
shallowShare <- mean(simPtr$Nature[!simPtr$deep] != 0)
deepShare <- mean(simPtr$Nature[simPtr$deep] != 0)
deepNeg <- simPtr$Year[simPtr$deep & simPtr$Nature == -1]
shallowCold <- coldYears[coldYears %in% simPtr$Year[!simPtr$deep]]
```

Before the collection reaches `r minDepth` series, `r pct(shallowShare)` of the years are pointer years. After, `r pct(deepShare)` are. Of the planted years, `r words(length(shallowCold))` fall in the shallow part: `r paste(shallowCold, collapse = ", ")`. `pointer` found them, but with the depth rule I'd set them aside along with the false ones, which is the cost of the rule.

@fig-ev-sim-pointer shows the percentage of series that dropped in each year.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ev-sim-pointer
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of simulated series whose ring was at least 10% narrower than the year before. Black bars are negative pointer years (75% or more), gray bars the rest. Dotted lines mark the eight planted cold years. The dashed line is the number of series, on the same scale, and the gray band covers the years with fewer than 13 series."
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(simPtr, aes(x = Year)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = min(simPtr$Year), xmax = max(simPtr$Year[!simPtr$deep]),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey90") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coldYears, linetype = 3) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = Year, y = 0, yend = Perc.neg,
                   colour = Nature == -1)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Nb.series), linetype = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey60", "black"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Series that dropped (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### What the Other Pointer Years Are

Where the depth is good, `pointer` still finds negative pointer years I didn't plant: `r length(setdiff(deepNeg, coldYears))` of them, against `r sum(coldYears %in% deepNeg)` planted. They aren't mistakes. The climate is the one thing all the trees share, and the simulation knows it, so I can look at what the climate did in those years.

```{r}
#| label: ev-sim-extra
simClim <- sim$truth$climate$climate / sd(sim$truth$climate$climate)
names(simClim) <- sim$truth$climate$year
extraNeg <- setdiff(deepNeg, coldYears)
extraLevel <- simClim[as.character(extraNeg)]
extraDrop <- simClim[as.character(extraNeg)] - simClim[as.character(extraNeg - 1)]
round(c(level = median(extraLevel), drop = median(extraDrop)), 2)
coldestOther <- names(which.min(simClim[!names(simClim) %in% coldYears]))
```

In the median unplanted pointer year the climate was `r abs(round(median(extraLevel), 2))` standard deviations below its mean, and `r abs(round(median(extraDrop), 2))` below the year before. The second number is what `pointer` responds to. A year of middling climate after a very good one can be a pointer year, and a cold year after another cold year can be missed. One of the extra years, `r coldestOther`, is the coldest year in the simulated climate that I didn't plant, `r abs(round(simClim[coldestOther], 2))` standard deviations below the mean. The random draw put it there.

Positive pointer years have a source of their own. After a narrow ring, a merely average one is a jump. The year after each planted cold year, a median `r round(median(simPtr$Perc.pos[match(coldYears + 1, simPtr$Year)]))`% of the series grew 10% or more, and `r words(sum(simPtr$Nature[match(coldYears + 1, simPtr$Year)] == 1, na.rm = TRUE))` of those years made the 75% cut. The trees' memory holds the recovery back: a bad year leaves some of its mark on the next ring, so the rebound is spread over a few years.

### A Sensitive Site

Mesa Verde's Douglas-firs are among the most sensitive trees in the book. Their ring widths swing from year to year, so a 10% change is the normal state of things.

```{r}
#| label: ev-co021-sensitivity
coMat <- as.matrix(co021)
coRatio <- coMat[-1, ] / coMat[-nrow(coMat), ]
coFinite <- coRatio[is.finite(coRatio) & coRatio > 0]
c(changed10 = mean(coFinite >= 1.1 | coFinite <= 0.9),
  medianChange = median(abs(coFinite - 1)))
```

`r pct(mean(coFinite >= 1.1 | coFinite <= 0.9))` of Mesa Verde's ring-to-ring ratios are a change of 10% or more, and the median change is `r pct(median(abs(coFinite - 1)))`. At the default settings most years are pointer years. Here's how many are, among the years with at least `r minDepth` series, at four values of `rgv.thresh`.

```{r}
#| label: ev-co021-pointer
coDeep <- function(rgv) {
  p <- pointer(co021, rgv.thresh = rgv)
  p <- p[p$Nb.series >= minDepth, ]
  c(rgv.thresh = rgv, years = nrow(p),
    positive = sum(p$Nature == 1), negative = sum(p$Nature == -1))
}
coTable <- t(sapply(c(10, 25, 50, 75), coDeep))
coTable
```

At 10%, `r coTable[1, "positive"] + coTable[1, "negative"]` of `r coTable[1, "years"]` years are pointer years, `r pct((coTable[1, "positive"] + coTable[1, "negative"]) / coTable[1, "years"])`. A list that long doesn't point at anything. At 50% there are `r coTable[3, "negative"]` negative ones, and at 75% `r coTable[4, "negative"]`. @Schweingruber1990 [p. 20] say the threshold depends on the aim and the trees, as low as 20% of series for trees at alpine treeline and 50% or more in semi-arid places. The same goes for `rgv.thresh`. Pick it from how much the site's rings vary, and say what you picked.

Mesa Verde has another thing `pointer` has to cope with: `r format(sum(co021 == 0, na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")` rings of zero width, the locally absent rings from [Crossdating](05Crossdating.qmd). A zero ring gives a ratio of 0, a drop. The ring after it gives a ratio of infinity, a jump, and two zeros in a row give 0/0, which isn't a number and is left out. The percentages handle that sensibly, but the mean and standard deviation of the ratios don't.

```{r}
#| label: ev-co021-zeros
coPtr <- pointer(co021)
sum(!is.finite(coPtr$RGV_mean))
```

In `r sum(!is.finite(coPtr$RGV_mean))` years `RGV_mean` is infinite. If you use those columns on a site with absent rings, check them first.

## Superposed Epoch Analysis

Superposed epoch analysis starts from the events. You pick a set of key years, line up the chronology around each one, and average across them. Lag 0 is the event year, lag 1 the year after, lag −1 the year before. If the events affect growth, the average at some lags should differ from the average of the chronology. To judge how much it differs, you do the same with key years drawn at random, many times over.

`sea` scales the chronology to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, so the averages are in standard units, and draws `resample = 1000` random sets of key years (with replacement, from the years at least `lag` from either end). For each lag, `p` is the share of random sets whose average was at least as extreme as the observed one, in the same direction. The confidence bands are the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the random averages, and the 0.5% and 99.5% ones.

### Planted Cold Years Again

```{r}
#| label: ev-sea-sim
simCrn <- chron(detrend(simRwl, method = "ModNegExp"))
set.seed(2)
simSea <- sea(simCrn, coldYears, lag = 5)
round(simSea[, 1:4], 3)
```

`se` is the scaled average at each lag and `se.unscaled` the same in index units. The planted years show up at lag 0, `r abs(round(simSea$se[simSea$lag == 0], 2))` standard deviations below the mean, and the trees' memory carries the drop into lag 1 (`r round(simSea$se[simSea$lag == 1], 2)`) and lag 2 (`r round(simSea$se[simSea$lag == 2], 2)`). Before the event, `r words(sum(simSea$p[simSea$lag < 0] < 0.05))` of the five lags have a `p` below 0.05. @fig-ev-sea-sim shows it.

```{r}
#| label: ev-sea-plot-fun
# plot sea output: bars for each lag, the 95% and 99% bands as lines
plotSea <- function(s) {
  ggplot(s, aes(x = lag, y = se)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_col(aes(fill = p < 0.05), width = 0.7) +
    geom_line(aes(y = ci.95.lower), linetype = 2) +
    geom_line(aes(y = ci.95.upper), linetype = 2) +
    geom_line(aes(y = ci.99.lower), linetype = 3) +
    geom_line(aes(y = ci.99.upper), linetype = 3) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "black"),
                      guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = s$lag) +
    labs(x = "Lag (years from the key year)",
         y = "Scaled chronology") +
    theme_minimal()
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ev-sea-sim
#| fig-cap: "Superposed epoch analysis of the simulated chronology at the eight planted cold years. Black bars have p below 0.05. Dashed lines are the 95% band from 1,000 sets of random years, dotted lines the 99% band."
#| fig-height: 3
plotSea(simSea)
```

### Finding Something in Nothing

Now the other direction. Here is a chronology of white noise the length of `cana157`, with 26 key years drawn at random (as many as the cold-year test below uses), run through `sea` 200 times. There's nothing to find.

```{r}
#| label: ev-sea-null
canaYears <- as.numeric(rownames(cana157))
set.seed(3)
seaNull <- t(replicate(200, {
  noise <- data.frame(std = rnorm(length(canaYears)), row.names = canaYears)
  key <- sample(canaYears[6:(length(canaYears) - 5)], 26)
  s <- sea(noise, key, lag = 5)
  c(lag0 = s$p[s$lag == 0] < 0.05, anyLag = any(s$p < 0.05),
    lag0half = s$p[s$lag == 0] < 0.025, anyLagHalf = any(s$p < 0.025))
}))
colMeans(seaNull)
```

At lag 0, `r pct(mean(seaNull[, "lag0"]))` of the runs had `p` below 0.05. That's about twice 5% because `p` is measured in whichever direction the average went: a low average is tested against the low tail and a high one against the high tail. So `p < 0.05` from `sea` is a two-sided test at 10%. Halve the cutoff, `p < 0.025`, for a two-sided test at 5%, and `r pct(mean(seaNull[, "lag0half"]))` of the runs pass.

The bigger problem is the number of lags. With 11 lags, `r pct(mean(seaNull[, "anyLag"]))` of the runs had at least one below 0.05, and `r pct(mean(seaNull[, "anyLagHalf"]))` had one below 0.025. A single significant lag somewhere in the window is what noise looks like. Decide which lags matter before you run it, from what you know of how the trees respond.

### Eruptions at Twisted Tree Heartrot Hill

`cana157` is a white spruce chronology from Twisted Tree Heartrot Hill in the Yukon, `r min(canaYears)` to `r max(canaYears)` [@Jacoby1992cana157]. Its first column is the standard chronology and its second the sample depth. Trees at the northern limit are often held back by cool summers, so cold years after big eruptions are a natural test.

The key years come from @Briffa1998, who built a hemisphere-wide record of summer warmth from a network of tree-ring density chronologies across the northern boreal forest. Their Table 2 lists the largest eruptions since 1400. Five of them they tie to cold summers in their record: Huaynaputina (1600, cold in 1601), Parker (1641), Tambora (1815, cold in 1816), Krakatau (1883, cold in 1884) and Novarupta (1912) (p. 452-453).

```{r}
#| label: ev-cana-volc
volcYears <- c(1601, 1641, 1816, 1884, 1912)
set.seed(4)
canaVolc <- sea(cana157, volcYears, lag = 5)
round(canaVolc[canaVolc$lag %in% 0:2, 1:4], 3)
```

Nothing. The scaled average at lag 0 is `r round(canaVolc$se[canaVolc$lag == 0], 2)`, with `p` = `r round(canaVolc$p[canaVolc$lag == 0], 2)`. Five years is a small set, and they don't agree: of the five, `r words(sum(scale(cana157[[1]])[match(volcYears, canaYears)] < 0))` are below the chronology's mean.

Their Table 1 is a longer list, the 30 years of lowest density in the whole record (p. 450). I keep the ones in `cana157`'s range.

```{r}
#| label: ev-cana-cold
# Briffa et al. (1998), Table 1: the 30 lowest years of NHD1, in rank order
briffaCold <- c(1601, 1816, 1641, 1453, 1817, 1695, 1912, 1675, 1698, 1643,
                1699, 1666, 1884, 1978, 1837, 1669, 1587, 1740, 1448, 1992,
                1836, 1818, 1495, 1968, 1742, 1783, 1667, 1642, 1819, 1446)
coldKeys <- sort(briffaCold[briffaCold >= min(canaYears)])
set.seed(5)
canaCold <- sea(cana157, coldKeys, lag = 10)
round(canaCold[, 1:4], 3)
```

That drops `r words(length(briffaCold) - length(coldKeys))` years before `cana157` starts and leaves `r length(coldKeys)`. I used a wider window, 10 years each side, because of what the default window of 5 shows: the average falls from lag 0 and is lowest at its edge. @fig-ev-sea-cana has the whole thing.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ev-sea-cana
#| fig-cap: "Superposed epoch analysis of cana157 at the 26 coldest summers in Briffa et al. (1998) that fall in its range. Black bars have p below 0.05. Dashed lines are the 95% band from 1,000 sets of random years, dotted lines the 99% band."
#| fig-height: 3
plotSea(canaCold)
```

The chronology is below average `r if (all(canaCold$se[canaCold$lag >= 0] < 0)) "at every lag from 0 to 10" else paste("at", words(sum(canaCold$se[canaCold$lag >= 0] < 0)), "of the 11 lags from 0 to 10")`, lowest at lag `r canaCold$lag[which.min(canaCold$se)]` (`r round(min(canaCold$se), 2)`). At lag 0, `p` is `r round(canaCold$p[canaCold$lag == 0], 3)`, which is above 0.025, and the strongest response is five years later.

Before reading that as a slow response to cold summers, look at the key years. Of the `r length(coldKeys)`, `r sum(diff(coldKeys) <= 3)` come within three years of the one before: 1641, 1642 and 1643; 1666, 1667 and 1669; 1816 through 1819. Cold summers come in runs, so a run of four keys counts the same cold spell four times, and their windows overlap. That's also why lag −1 is low (`r round(canaCold$se[canaCold$lag == -1], 2)`): in a run, the year before one key is often another key. `sea`'s random years are drawn one at a time and don't come in runs, so the random averages vary less than averages of clustered keys would, and the bands are too narrow.

A fairer comparison keeps the spacing of the keys and moves them all together. Shift the whole set by some number of years, wrapping years that fall off the end back to the start, and compute the same averages. Here are all the shifts more than 10 years from the listed dates.

```{r}
#| label: ev-cana-shift
canaScaled <- as.numeric(scale(cana157[[1]]))
nCana <- length(canaYears)
epoch <- function(keys, lags = -10:10) {
  sapply(lags, function(l) {
    i <- (keys + l - min(canaYears)) %% nCana + 1   # wrap around the ends
    mean(canaScaled[i])
  })
}
observed <- epoch(coldKeys)
shifts <- 11:(nCana - 11)
shifted <- t(sapply(shifts, function(k) epoch(coldKeys + k)))
shiftP <- colMeans(sweep(shifted, 2, observed, "<="))
names(shiftP) <- -10:10
round(shiftP[as.character(0:10)], 3)
```

`shiftP` is the share of the `r length(shifts)` shifted sets with an average as low as the observed one. At lag 0 it's `r round(shiftP["0"], 3)`, and at lag 5 it's `r round(shiftP["5"], 3)`, `r sum(shifted[, 16] <= observed[16])` of `r length(shifts)` shifts. With the runs kept in the comparison, the low growth after the cold years still stands out.

The runs can still do the work another way. A run of cold summers is a cold spell, and a cold spell gives several years of low growth whether or not any one summer leaves a mark of its own. So here is the same shift test with only the first year of each run as a key.

```{r}
#| label: ev-cana-decluster
firstOfRun <- coldKeys[c(TRUE, diff(coldKeys) > 3)]
firstOfRun
observedFirst <- epoch(firstOfRun)
shiftedFirst <- t(sapply(shifts, function(k) epoch(firstOfRun + k)))
shiftPFirst <- colMeans(sweep(shiftedFirst, 2, observedFirst, "<="))
firstTable <- rbind(average = observedFirst, shiftP = shiftPFirst)
colnames(firstTable) <- -10:10
round(firstTable[, as.character(-1:10)], 3)
meanFirst <- mean(observedFirst[11:21])                  # lags 0 to 10
meanFirstP <- mean(rowMeans(shiftedFirst[, 11:21]) <= meanFirst)
```

With `r length(firstOfRun)` keys, one per run, the picture changes. Lags 1 to 3 are near or above average. The low at lag 5 is still there (`r round(observedFirst[16], 2)`, `shiftP` `r round(shiftPFirst[16], 3)`), and so is one at lag −1, the year before the cold summer (`r format(round(observedFirst[10], 2), nsmall = 2)`, `r round(shiftPFirst[10], 3)`). Two lags of 21 with `p` near 0.01 or 0.02 is about what [Finding Something in Nothing](#finding-something-in-nothing) says noise gives. Over lags 0 to 10 the average is `r round(meanFirst, 2)`, and `r pct(meanFirstP)` of the shifted sets are as low.

What do I make of it? Growth at Twisted Tree Heartrot Hill is low during the cold spells in Briffa's list, which fall in the 1640s, 1660s, 1690s and 1810s. Briffa and colleagues find the 1810s the coldest decade in their record (p. 452). Whether a single cold summer leaves a mark of its own in these ring widths, this test can't easily tell: with one key per run, the pattern by lag is about what noise looks like. One more caution. Their map of sites (Fig. 2) has a dense cluster in Alaska and northwestern Canada. If some are near `cana157`, the keys were picked partly from the same region's summers. That's fine for asking whether this site responds to cold that reached across the hemisphere, and it means the keys and the chronology aren't fully independent.

## Choosing

Use `pointer` when you want the years the trees agree on, with no list in hand. Set `rgv.thresh` from how much the site's rings vary, set aside years with fewer than about 13 series, and remember that a pointer year is a change from the year before. On a site with absent rings, check `RGV_mean` and `RGV_sd` for infinite values.

Use `sea` when you have a list of events chosen without looking at the chronology. Read its `p` as two-sided at twice the value, choose the lags you care about in advance, and look at how the key years are spaced. If they come in runs, compare against shifted copies of the whole set instead of independent random years, and try again with one key per run.

For both, plant some events in a simulated stand like the one here and see whether your settings find them. It takes a few lines and tells you what your choices can see.

## Wrapping Up

Pointer years start from the trees. `pointer` counts the share of series whose ring changed by more than a threshold from the year before. It found most of the cold years planted in a simulated stand, along with a good many years of ordinary bad climate, and more where only a few series were in. At a site as sensitive as Mesa Verde the default threshold makes most years pointer years, so the thresholds have to fit the site.

Superposed epoch analysis starts from the events. `sea` recovered the planted cold years and the trees' memory after them. On white noise it found a significant lag in most runs, because its `p` is one-sided in the observed direction and the window holds 11 lags. On `cana157`, growth is low during the runs of cold summers in Briffa's list, and that holds up against shifted key sets that keep the runs together. With one key per run most of the response goes away, so it's the cold spells, more than the single summers, that show in these ring widths.

[Python and dplPy](17DplPy.qmd) is next.

## Exercises

1. Rerun the simulated stand with `phi = 0` in `sim.collection`, so the trees have no memory. What happens to lags 1 and 2 in `sea`, and to the positive pointer years after each cold year?
2. Change `nseries.thresh` and `rgv.thresh` in `pointer` on the simulated stand and count planted and unplanted negative pointer years where at least 13 series are in. Which settings find all five planted years in that part with the fewest others?
3. Run `pointer` on `wa082`. How sensitive are its rings by the measure used for Mesa Verde, and what `rgv.thresh` gives a list of pointer years you could check by eye?
4. Repeat the white-noise check with 5 key years instead of 26. Does the share of runs with a significant lag change?
5. Take the 26 cold years and keep only those that are not followed by another key year within five years. Run `sea` on `cana157` with that set. Does the response at lag 5 survive?

## Further Reading

- @Schweingruber1990 set out the terms, event year, pointer year and pointer interval, and has the formula for how many series must agree. It's also a guide to drawing event years by hand, from skeleton plots.
- @Becker1994 is the source of the rule `pointer` uses, applied to oaks in northeastern France.
- @Briffa1998 is the source of the cold years, and a good read on how hard it is to tie a cold summer to a particular eruption.
- @SwetnamBrown2011 [p. 268-270] use superposed epoch analysis to show that fire years in the American Southwest tend to follow wet years, and @Speer2010 [p. 231-233] walks through the method.
